entry.title: Fastest Soft Robot Ever Built Doesn’t Need Electronics to Function

media:group.media:title: Fastest Soft Robot Ever Built Doesn’t Need Electronics to Function
media:group.media:description:
The fastest robot to be made entirely of soft materials can reach speeds of up to 4.72 meters – a little more than 5 yards – per second, engineers at the University of California San Diego have shown. The six-legged robot can run on a wide range of terrain, from sand, to mulch, to concrete. It can also swim in water and walk underwater. The robot, designed, built and tested at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering, is 3D-printed in one go using only one material and doesn’t need electronics to function.
https://today.ucsd.edu/story/the-fastest-soft-robot-ever-built-doesnt-need-electronics-to-function
DOI 10.1126/scirobotics.aei1264 Yichen Zhai and Mike Tolley Bioinspired Robotics and Design Lab https://bioinspired.ucsd.edu
Jacobs School of Engineering University of California San Diego
Accessible version: https://youtu.be/uNPwgYMA0Js

entry.title: Researchers use a physical device to take over electronics in a Boeing 737

media:group.media:title: Researchers use a physical device to take over electronics in a Boeing 737
media:group.media:description:
Computer science researchers developed and tested a device that, if plugged into a hardwired communications channel connecting two key flight computers, can take over communications between these computers. The proof-of-concept attack suggests that physical access to an aircraft’s computer bay under the nose of the plane is a cybersecurity risk that should be considered.
The device needs to be plugged into a port inside the plane’s belly – an action that the researchers estimate would take under 60 seconds. This would require access to the aircraft either when parked at a gate or when in an airport hangar during regular maintenance. Access to these areas is controlled carefully but not always successfully. The researchers successfully demonstrated the attack on a testbed made of actual Boeing 737 airplane parts and airplane software.
https://today.ucsd.edu/story/researchers-use-a-physical-device-to-take-over-electronics-in-a-boeing-737

entry.title: Soft robot removes mock blood clot from phantom model

media:group.media:title: Soft robot removes mock blood clot from phantom model
media:group.media:description:
A research team led by Tania Morimoto, associate professor of mechanical and aerospace engineering at UC San Diego, was awarded up to $22.9M from ARPA-H to develop a soft, flexible robot that can safely and autonomously navigate through the tiny blood vessels of the brain and remove a blood clot, expanding access to life-saving stroke care.
The breakthrough idea that enables this robot to safely and compliantly navigate the vasculature is that it turns its skin inside out, unfurling from its tip to grow, rather than being pushed from its base.
Researchers in Morimoto’s lab have already demonstrated that this type of growing robot could successfully navigate a model of human blood vessels, as shown in the video.
This video is from the paper "Serially-Connected Soft Continuum Robots for Endovascular Emergencies," published in IEEE Transactions on Medical Robotics and Bionics (2025).
Paper authors: A. Mangan, S. Kim, N. Jones, M.G. Brandel, J.J. Heit, A. Norbash, J.T. Hwang, E. Hawkes, and T.K. Morimoto.
Video courtesy of the Morimoto Lab.

entry.title: 2 Million Cars with Anti-Theft Systems Installed by Dealers are at Higher Risk of Theft

media:group.media:title: 2 Million Cars with Anti-Theft Systems Installed by Dealers are at Higher Risk of Theft
media:group.media:description:
At least 2.2 million cars on the road today are vulnerable to an attack that allows thieves to lock and unlock doors and immobilize vehicle engines remotely via a Bluetooth connection, computer scientists at the University of California San Diego have found.
Attackers can get access to cars from as far as five yards away. Most of the vulnerable vehicles were bought at Honda, Toyota, Mazda, Ford, and Jeep dealerships in Southern California from 2017 to today. But because these vehicles are resold on the second-hand market, several hundred thousand vulnerable vehicles can also be found throughout the United States, Canada and even as far as Japan. Many vulnerable cars display a sticker with the word “KARR” or “SWDS” on the driver’s-side window.
The company manufacturing these devices, Acrisure, is releasing a patch to fix the vulnerability on July 20, 2026. The fix requires downloading an app or visiting a dealer. “Many car owners don’t even know that their vehicle is vulnerable. So we wanted to make sure they were aware by publishing this study,” said Aaron Schulman, a professor in the UC San Diego Department of Computer Science and Engineering, and one of the study’s senior authors.

entry.title: Surgeons Use Teleoperated Humanoid Robots to Perform Live Surgery – a World First. EAD version

entry.title: Engineers Shake Tallest Steel-framed Building Ever to be Built on an Earthquake Simulator

media:group.media:title: Engineers Shake Tallest Steel-framed Building Ever to be Built on an Earthquake Simulator
media:group.media:description:
A 10-story, 100-foot structure was experiencing simulations of real earthquakes, including the 6.9 magnitude, 1989 Loma Prieta temblor, as part of an effort to determine if height limits for buildings made of cold-formed steel should be increased. entry.title: Material model adapts stiffness using sound waves

media:group.media:title: Material model adapts stiffness using sound waves
media:group.media:description:
Using this model of a 1D material, researchers demonstrate a new way to remotely change a material's stiffness using sound waves. The team was co-led by the University of California San Diego, University of Michigan, and the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS) at Laboratory of Acoustics of Le Mans University.
Video with extended audio descriptions available here: https://youtu.be/TjNHbeUOhfk

entry.title: First-of-its-kind cleanroom turns inventions into devices ready for FDA approval

media:group.media:title: First-of-its-kind cleanroom turns inventions into devices ready for FDA approval
media:group.media:description:
Take a tour in UC San Diego's new good manufacturing practices facility. The space is dedicated to building devices that can be implanted in the human body – especially for neurological applications. Located at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering, the facility meets strict standards and regulations needed for approvals by the Food and Drug Administration for devices implanted in the human body.
Video with extended audio descriptions available here: https://youtu.be/GbkJKAHntqM

media:group.media:title: 2025 Jacobs School of Engineering Highlights
media:group.media:description:
Before we dive into a new quarter and a new year, we're taking a moment to reflect on some Jacobs School of Engineering highlights from 2025. Last year, the Jacobs School:
🔹Ranked Top 10 (yet again!) 🔹Launched an AI major 🔹Doubled our bioengineering instructional lab capacity 🔹Initiated a semiconductor workforce development pilot with NSF funding
The Jacobs School welcomed new faculty and contributed 2,800 computer scientists and engineers to the innovation workforce. We powered emerging industries including fusion engineering, healthcare engineering, biomanufacturing, and AI.
Our research drives real-world impact, and in 2025 led to safer and more resilient buildings; an understanding of what's driving a colorectal cancer epidemic; and more secure satellite communications.
Thank you to everyone inside and outside the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering for your excellence, hard work and generosity! This video is just a taste of what we are accomplishing together.

entry.title: Researchers test a 10-story, cold-formed steel building for resiliency to fires and earthquakes

media:group.media:title: Researchers test a 10-story, cold-formed steel building for resiliency to fires and earthquakes
media:group.media:description:
When a 10-story test building in San Diego shook and twisted this summer, it wasn’t because of a real earthquake — it was part of a federally funded experiment designed to make future buildings safer when the next big one strikes.
A few weeks later, smoke and flames fanned out the window of the building's ninth floor. The researchers had returned for fire testing to see how a building damaged by earthquakes would withstand a blaze.
The structure was built this year at the UC San Diego earthquake simulator located in the Scripps Ranch neighborhood of San Diego. Funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), the facility is one of the three largest shake table facilities in the world and the only one located outdoors. The simulator, part of UC San Diego’s Englekirk Structural Engineering Center, is capable of shaking structures in six directions: back and forth, up and down, left to right, and in the three rotational movements of yaw, pitch and roll.
Extended audio description version available here: https://youtu.be/Kuw24NLD2lo

entry.title: Air Pollution Linked to Mutations That May BeDriving Lung Cancer in Never-smokers (Full Q&A w subs)

media:group.media:title: Air Pollution Linked to Mutations That May BeDriving Lung Cancer in Never-smokers (Full Q&A w subs)
media:group.media:description: A new study reveals that air pollution, traditional herbal medicines and other environmental exposures are linked to genetic mutations that may contribute to the development of lung cancer in people with no or hardly any history of smoking. Ludmil Alexandrov, study co-senior author and professor in the Shu Chien-Gene Lay Department of Bioengineering and the Department of Cellular and Molecular Medicine at UC San Diego, explains these findings in more detail.
